**Question:** Under water, pressure increases by $1\text{ atm}$ for a $33\text{ ft}$ ($10\text{ m}$) increase of depth. The divers have gone a maximum depth of $1000\text{ ft}$ ($330\text{ m}$), how much pressure did they have to tolerate?

**Answer:** Per $10\text{ m}$ depth, pressure increases by $1\text{ atm}$ or $1\text{ bar}$. Then, for $330\text{ m}$ depth,
$$\frac{330\text{ m}}{10\text{ m/atm}} = 33\text{ atm}$$

Divers had to tolerate $33\text{ atm}$ pressure.

**Question:** Calculate the pressure at a depth of $50\text{ cm}$ for kerosene (density $800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$), water (density $1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}$) and mercury (density $13600\text{ kg m}^{-3}$).

**Answer:** For kerosene,
$$\text{pressure, } p = h\rho g$$
$$P = 0.50\text{ m} \times 800\text{ kg m}^{-3} \times 9.8\text{ N kg}^{-1} = 3,920\text{ N m}^{-2}$$

For water,
$$P = 0.50\text{ m} \times 1000\text{ kg m}^{-3} \times 9.8\text{ N kg}^{-1} = 4,900\text{ N m}^{-2}$$

For mercury,
$$P = 0.50\text{ m} \times 13,600\text{ kg m}^{-3} \times 9.8\text{ N kg}^{-1} = 66,640\text{ N m}^{-2}$$

**Question:** At what depth of the liquids kerosene, water and mercury pressure will be $1\text{ atm}$ ?

**Answer:** We know, for mercury pressure is $1\text{ atm}$ at a depth of $76\text{ cm}$. Density of water is $13.6$ times less than mercury, therefore depth of water will be $13.6$ times more.

Therefore, depth for water: $76\text{ cm} \times 13.6 = 1034\text{ cm} = 10.34\text{ m}$

Density of kerosene is $0.8$ times less than water, therefore depth for kerosene will be $1/0.8 = 1.25$ times more.

Therefore, depth for kerosene: $10.34\text{ m} \times 1.25 = 12.92\text{ m}$
